blocks.text: A prefix sum query computes the sum of all elements from index 1 through index i, using the Fenwick tree's standard 1-indexed convention. This topic focuses specifically on the query side, computing prefix sums and, by extension, arbitrary range sums, assuming you already understand the general Fenwick tree structure from the introduction topic.

The update and query walks move in OPPOSITE directions through the lowbit trick: update ADDS lowbit to move toward larger indices, query SUBTRACTS lowbit to move toward zero. This directional mirror is one of the most important things to internalize about how Fenwick trees work.

blocks.caption: Starting at index 6, repeatedly subtracting lowbit visits index 6, then 4, then reaches 0, where the accumulated sum equals the full prefix sum.

blocks.text: Starting at index i, repeatedly SUBTRACT the lowbit of i from i, moving to i minus lowbit(i), accumulating that node's stored value into a running total at each step, until i reaches 0. Subtracting lowbit always moves toward smaller indices, guaranteeing the walk terminates once it reaches 0.
The nodes visited during this descent are exactly the set whose stored partial sums, added together, reconstruct the full prefix sum up to index i, no more, no less.

content.title: 2. Update vs Query: The Directional Mirror

blocks.caption: Update moves upward by adding lowbit; query moves downward by subtracting lowbit. Internalizing this mirror image is the single most useful mental shortcut for Fenwick trees.
blocks.alt: Update vs Query: The Directional Mirror

blocks.text: This is worth stating as a memorable rule on its own: whenever you are unsure which direction a Fenwick tree operation should move, remember that UPDATE goes UP (adds lowbit, toward larger indices, propagating a change to every range that includes the updated position) and QUERY goes DOWN (subtracts lowbit, toward zero, gathering every partial sum that together cover the prefix).

Computing prefixSum(6) on an 8 element array: start at i=6, lowbit(6) is 2 (110 in binary, lowest set bit is the 2s place), subtract to get i=4, add tree[6] to the running total. Next, lowbit(4) is 4 (100 in binary), subtract to get i=0, add tree[4] to the running total. The loop ends since i=0. The final result is tree[6] + tree[4].

Confirming correctness: if the underlying array (1-indexed) is [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6], the manual prefix sum from index 1 through 6 is 3+1+4+1+5+9 = 23. The Fenwick tree, by construction, stores tree[4] as the sum of indices 1 through 4 (3+1+4+1=9) and tree[6] as the sum of indices 5 through 6 (5+9=14), and 9+14 = 23, matching exactly.

The sum from index L to R equals prefixSum(R) minus prefixSum(L-1). This is standard prefix sum arithmetic: prefixSum(R) includes everything from 1 through R, and subtracting prefixSum(L-1) removes everything from 1 through L-1, leaving exactly the range L through R.
The subtraction uses L-1, not L, specifically because you want to EXCLUDE index L-1 and everything before it, while still INCLUDING index L itself in the final range sum.

Each prefix sum query runs in O(log n) time, the same bound as an update, for the same reason: the lowbit walk length is bounded by the number of bits in the array size, regardless of whether the walk moves up (update) or down (query).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Query cost","Update cost"],"rows":[["Raw prefix sum array","O(1)","O(n), every subsequent prefix must be recomputed"],["Naive per-query sum","O(n), no preprocessing needed","O(1)"],["Fenwick tree","O(log n)","O(log n)"]]}

blocks.text: Neither extreme alternative balances both operations well. A raw prefix sum array is ideal only when the array never changes. A naive per query sum is ideal only when updates vastly outnumber queries. A Fenwick tree exists precisely because most real problems need BOTH operations to be reasonably fast, and O(log n) for both is the balanced compromise.

Mixing up the update direction (adding lowbit) with the query direction (subtracting lowbit): applying the wrong direction for a given operation either visits the wrong nodes entirely or, in the worst case, causes an infinite loop.
Forgetting the L-1 in the range query formula: writing rangeSum as prefixSum(r) minus prefixSum(l) instead of prefixSum(l-1) incorrectly excludes index l from the result.

Calling prefixSum with index 0 expecting a meaningful non zero result: prefixSum(0) is defined to return 0 by construction, the loop condition i > 0 causes it to exit immediately without accumulating anything, which is the correct base case, not a bug.

Range Sum Query Mutable is the direct application, combining this topic with the sibling point update topic. Range Sum Query 2D Mutable extends the same idea to a 2D Fenwick tree as a more advanced variant. Count of Smaller Numbers After Self is a less obvious but classic Fenwick tree application, using it to count elements rather than sum values, worth knowing the same prefix query mechanics generalize beyond pure summation.
